title: Backtesting a pair
objectives: Backtest a pair with costs and no look-ahead.
Check a backtest by changing the future and watching the past.

screens.title: One of them cheated
screens.prose: Two backtests of `make_pair(3, 1500)` with lesson 9's rules: entry ±2, exit 0, stop ±4, 5 bp costs. A earns £37.29 with Sharpe 1.647. B earns £28.56 with Sharpe 1.124. One fitted its hedge ratio and $z$ on all 1,500 days at once.
screens.question: Which backtest used information it could not have had?

options.text: A: a fit on all 1,500 days tells day 300 about days 301 to 1,499
B, since its P&L is lower
options.why: A lower P&L is no sign of cheating. Cheating usually makes a backtest look better.

options.text: Neither: using more data gives a better estimate
options.why: More data is better only if it existed at the time. On day 300, days 301 to 1,499 had not happened.

hints.text: Which backtest knows the future?
A fit on all 1,500 days uses prices after the day being traded.
A knew where the spread's mean and sd would settle; B used only the past 250 days.

feedback.correct: Correct. A had look-ahead; B is the honest one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which fit used days after the trading day.

byKey.B: You took the lower result as the suspect. Look-ahead almost always flatters a backtest.

explain.text: A's $\alpha$, $\beta$ and sd came from all 1,500 days, so every early trade knew the spread's long-run mean. That foresight is worth £8.73 and 0.52 of Sharpe here. B is lesson 9's reference backtest, which uses only the past.

options.text: It falls by about £2.64 for every 5 bp, in a straight line
Hardly at all: 5 bp is tiny
options.why: At 40 bp the P&L is £10.05, a third of the cost-free £31.21.

options.text: Nothing until a threshold, then it collapses
options.why: Step through the costs: each 5 bp takes the same amount.

hints.text: Read the caption at 0, 5 and 10 bp.
Each 5 bp takes about £2.64: the trades are the same, only their cost changes.

feedback.correct: That's it. The same 25 changes pay a cost that grows in proportion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the caption's P&L at each step.

explain.text: The trades do not change with the cost, so each basis point takes the same £0.53. The P&L would reach zero near 59 bp.

screens.title: Only the past
screens.prose: **No look-ahead**: every number used on day $t$ comes from days up to $t$. B fits $\alpha_t$, $\beta_t$ and the residual sd on the last 250 days, today included. It trades at day $t$'s close and earns from day $t + 1$. The hedge ratio is fixed when a trade opens.
screens.question: On day 700, what is the first day the rolling fit may use?

hints.text: The window holds 250 days and ends today.
From day $a$ to day 700 inclusive is $700 - a + 1$ days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count 250 days back from day 700, including day 700.

byKey.450: Days 450 to 700 are 251 days. Count day 700 itself.
byKey.0: Starting at day 0 is an expanding window. B's window rolls: it drops the oldest day each day.

screens.title: The rolling fit
screens.prose: Write the reference `rolling_fit`. On each day from `window - 1` on, fit $y$ on $x$ over the last `window` days, today included. Keep the intercept, the slope and the sample sd (`ddof=1`) of that window's residuals. Earlier days stay NaN.

    """alpha_t, beta_t and residual sd from OLS of y on x over days t - window + 1 to t."""
    a = np.full(len(y), np.nan); b = a.copy(); sd = a.copy()
    for t in range(window - 1, len(y)):
        xs, ys = ..., ...          # the last `window` days, today included
        bb, aa = np.polyfit(xs, ys, 1); r = ys - aa - bb * xs
        a[t], b[t], sd[t] = aa, bb, ...    # sample sd of r

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def rolling_fit(y, x, window):
    """alpha_t, beta_t and residual sd from OLS of y on x over days t - window + 1 to t."""
    a = np.full(len(y), np.nan); b = a.copy(); sd = a.copy()
    for t in range(window - 1, len(y)):
        xs, ys = x[t - window + 1:t + 1], y[t - window + 1:t + 1]
        bb, aa = np.polyfit(xs, ys, 1); r = ys - aa - bb * xs
        a[t], b[t], sd[t] = aa, bb, r.std(ddof=1)
    return a, b, sd

screens.title: The cost of a round trip
screens.prose: Open a long spread: buy one $y$ at £80.00 and sell $\beta = 1.5$ shares of $x$ at £50.00. Both shares have a 10 bp bid-ask spread. Each side of a trade costs half of it, as in the Microstructure course's lesson 5. Ignore price moves.
screens.question: What do opening and later closing this trade cost in pounds?

hints.text: Add the pounds traded in both legs.
£155 per side, at half of 10 bp, which is 5 bp.
Open and close: $2 \times 155 \times 5 / 10{,}000 = £0.155$.

feedback.correct: Correct. About £0.16 a round trip, which is B's 5 bp per change.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two legs, two sides, half the spread each time.

byKey.oneside: You costed the opening only. The close crosses the spread again.
byKey.oneleg: You costed only $y$. The hedge leg in $x$ crosses its spread too.
byKey.full: You charged the whole spread on each side. From the mid, each side costs half of it.

explain.text: Each side trades £80 + £75 = £155 and pays 5 bp, half of 10 bp: £0.0775. Opening and closing doubles it to £0.155. A pair pays this on two legs, which is why pairs feel costs more than one-share trades.

screens.title: Fit once, on everything
screens.prose: A colleague regresses $y$ on $x$ over all 1,500 days. He z-scores the residual with its full-sample mean and sd. "It is the best estimate of $\beta$ we have," he says. It earns Sharpe 1.647.
screens.question: What is wrong with it?

options.text: On day 300 its $\beta$, mean and sd already contain days 301 to 1,499: look-ahead
Nothing: a better $\beta$ is a better backtest
options.why: You judged the estimate, not the timing. The best estimate today cannot use prices from next year.

options.text: It must have left out the costs
options.why: It pays the same 5 bp per change. The gap comes from what the fit knew.

options.text: Its $\beta$ is wrong
options.why: Its $\beta$, 1.4888, is close to the true 1.5. The problem is when it could have been known.

hints.text: When was the full-sample $\beta$ known?
Only after day 1,499.
Every early trade used a number from the future.

feedback.correct: Correct. The full-sample fit is look-ahead, whatever its accuracy.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask on which day each number would have been known.

byKey.fine: You trusted the better estimate. It is better because it saw the future, which no live trader can.

explain.text: A full-sample fit tells each early day where the spread will settle, so entries and exits look sharper. That foresight lifts the Sharpe from 1.124 to 1.647. Level 2's lesson 6 found the same look-ahead in a full-sample z-score.

screens.title: The backtest in code
screens.prose: Write the P&L loop. Yesterday's holding earns today's hedged move, $u_{t-1}(\Delta y_t - h\,\Delta x_t)$, with $h$ the hedge ratio fixed at entry. A change pays `cost_bp` on the pounds traded in both legs. One flag switches to the cheating full-sample fit.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_two_walks(seed, n=500):
    """Two independent Gaussian random walks from 0 (columns of one draw)."""
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((n, 2))
    return np.cumsum(z[:, 0]), np.cumsum(z[:, 1])


def make_pair(seed, n=1000, alpha=5.0, beta=1.5, phi=0.95, sd_u=0.5, x0=40.0, vol=0.015):
    """A cointegrated pair of share prices in pounds. x starts at x0 and is a log random walk
    with daily sd vol; y = alpha + beta * x + u, u an AR(1) with coefficient phi and shock sd sd_u."""
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((n, 2))
    x = x0 * np.exp(np.cumsum(vol * z[:, 0]))
    u = np.empty(n); u[0] = sd_u * z[0, 1]
    for t in range(1, n):
        u[t] = phi * u[t - 1] + sd_u * z[t, 1]
    return x, alpha + beta * x + u


def make_broken_pair(seed, n=1500, break_at=1000, sd_break=1.0, **kw):
    """make_pair, plus a random walk added to y from day break_at: the spread stops reverting."""
    x, y = make_pair(seed, n, **kw)
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed + 1000).standard_normal(n)
    return x, y + np.concatenate([np.zeros(break_at), np.cumsum(sd_break * z[break_at:])])


def rolling_fit(y, x, window):
    """alpha_t, beta_t and residual sd from OLS of y on x over days t - window + 1 to t."""
    a = np.full(len(y), np.nan); b = a.copy(); sd = a.copy()
    for t in range(window - 1, len(y)):
        xs, ys = x[t - window + 1:t + 1], y[t - window + 1:t + 1]
        bb, aa = np.polyfit(xs, ys, 1); r = ys - aa - bb * xs
        a[t], b[t], sd[t] = aa, bb, r.std(ddof=1)
    return a, b, sd


def positions(z, entry=2.0, exit=0.0, stop=4.0):
    """+1 long the spread (long y, short beta x), -1 short, 0 flat; decided at each day's close."""
    pos = np.zeros(len(z)); cur = 0
    for t in range(len(z)):
        zt = z[t]
        if np.isnan(zt): cur = 0
        elif cur == 0:
            if entry <= zt < stop: cur = -1
            elif -stop < zt <= -entry: cur = 1
        elif cur == 1 and (zt >= -exit or zt <= -stop): cur = 0
        elif cur == -1 and (zt <= exit or zt >= stop): cur = 0
        pos[t] = cur
    return pos
widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def daily_pnl(y, x, window=250, entry=2.0, exit=0.0, stop=4.0, cost_bp=5.0, lookahead=False):
    """Daily P&L in pounds for one share of y, and the number of position changes."""
    y, x = np.asarray(y, float), np.asarray(x, float)
    if lookahead:      # the cheat: one fit on every day
        bb, aa = np.polyfit(x, y, 1); r = y - aa - bb * x
        a = np.full(len(y), aa); b = np.full(len(y), bb); sd = np.full(len(y), r.std(ddof=1))
    else:
        a, b, sd = rolling_fit(y, x, window)
    pos = positions((y - a - b * x) / sd, entry, exit, stop)
    n = len(y); pnl = np.zeros(n); units = 0.0; hb = 0.0; trades = 0
    for t in range(1, n):
        pnl[t] = ...       # yesterday's holding times today's hedged move
        if pos[t] != pos[t - 1]:
            new_hb = b[t] if pos[t] != 0 else 0.0
            traded = ...   # pounds traded in y and in x
            pnl[t] -= traded * cost_bp / 1e4; trades += 1
            units, hb = pos[t], new_hb
    return pnl, trades


def backtest(y, x, window=250, entry=2.0, exit=0.0, stop=4.0, cost_bp=5.0):
    pnl, trades = daily_pnl(y, x, window, entry, exit, stop, cost_bp)
    sharpe = pnl.mean() / pnl.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)
    return round(float(pnl.sum()), 2), round(float(sharpe), 3), trades


def lookahead_backtest(y, x, entry=2.0, exit=0.0, stop=4.0, cost_bp=5.0):
    pnl, trades = daily_pnl(y, x, 250, entry, exit, stop, cost_bp, lookahead=True)
    sharpe = pnl.mean() / pnl.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)
    return round(float(pnl.sum()), 2), round(float(sharpe), 3), trades
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def daily_pnl(y, x, window=250, entry=2.0, exit=0.0, stop=4.0, cost_bp=5.0, lookahead=False):
    """Daily P&L in pounds for one share of y, and the number of position changes."""
    y, x = np.asarray(y, float), np.asarray(x, float)
    if lookahead:      # the cheat: one fit on every day
        bb, aa = np.polyfit(x, y, 1); r = y - aa - bb * x
        a = np.full(len(y), aa); b = np.full(len(y), bb); sd = np.full(len(y), r.std(ddof=1))
    else:
        a, b, sd = rolling_fit(y, x, window)
    pos = positions((y - a - b * x) / sd, entry, exit, stop)
    n = len(y); pnl = np.zeros(n); units = 0.0; hb = 0.0; trades = 0
    for t in range(1, n):
        pnl[t] = units * ((y[t] - y[t - 1]) - hb * (x[t] - x[t - 1]))
        if pos[t] != pos[t - 1]:
            new_hb = b[t] if pos[t] != 0 else 0.0
            traded = abs(pos[t] - units) * y[t] + abs(pos[t] * new_hb - units * hb) * x[t]
            pnl[t] -= traded * cost_bp / 1e4; trades += 1
            units, hb = pos[t], new_hb
    return pnl, trades


def backtest(y, x, window=250, entry=2.0, exit=0.0, stop=4.0, cost_bp=5.0):
    pnl, trades = daily_pnl(y, x, window, entry, exit, stop, cost_bp)
    sharpe = pnl.mean() / pnl.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)
    return round(float(pnl.sum()), 2), round(float(sharpe), 3), trades


def lookahead_backtest(y, x, entry=2.0, exit=0.0, stop=4.0, cost_bp=5.0):
    pnl, trades = daily_pnl(y, x, 250, entry, exit, stop, cost_bp, lookahead=True)
    sharpe = pnl.mean() / pnl.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)
    return round(float(pnl.sum()), 2), round(float(sharpe), 3), trades

tests.call: bool(np.allclose(daily_pnl(y, x, lookahead=True)[0][:1000], daily_pnl(y2, x, lookahead=True)[0][:1000]))

explain.text: P&L on day $t$ uses the holding set at day $t - 1$'s close: no signal earns its own day. The future test is the strongest check: change the future, and the past must not move. The cheat fails it, because its one fit reads every day.

screens.title: Re-hedging every day
screens.prose: A tempting variant recomputes the spread each day as $y_t - \beta_t x_t$, with that day's rolling $\beta_t$. It z-scores it by its own 60-day mean and sd, and re-hedges daily. Before costs it loses £4.44, Sharpe −0.11. Lesson 9's rules earn £31.21 before costs.
screens.question: Why does the variant fail?

options.text: Each day's change in $\beta_t$, times a price near £70, moves its spread by about £0.17 of pure noise
It pays more costs
options.why: Both lines here are before costs. The variant loses money with costs at zero.

options.text: It has look-ahead
options.why: Every number in it comes from the past. It is honest, just badly built.

options.text: 60 days is too short for a z-score
options.why: Level 2's rolling z used 60 days. The fault is the moving $\beta_t$ inside the spread.

hints.text: What changes in $y_t - \beta_t x_t$ when $\beta_t$ changes?
$\beta_t$ moves by about 0.0025 a day on average; $x$ is about £70.
$0.0025 \times 70 \approx £0.17$ a day of spread movement that is only estimation noise.

feedback.correct: Correct. The spread's moves are partly the estimate moving, not the prices.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what a daily change in $\beta_t$ does to $y_t - \beta_t x_t$.

byKey.look: You suspected look-ahead. The variant is honest; its signal is noise.

explain.text: The variant's spread changes whenever the estimate does, by about £0.17 a day, and it drops the intercept $\alpha_t$. So its z-score tracks the fit, not the pair. Fixing $\beta$ at entry keeps each trade's spread a real position.

screens.title: Is 1.124 real?
screens.prose: B can trade from day 249 to day 1,499: 1,251 days, or $1{,}251/252 = 4.96$ years. The Testing course's lesson 11 gives a Sharpe ratio over $T$ years a standard error of about $1/\sqrt{T}$.
screens.question: How many standard errors is 1.124 from zero? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: $t = \text{SR}/\text{se} = \text{SR}\sqrt{T}$.

feedback.correct: Correct. About 2.5 standard errors: evidence, not proof.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the Sharpe by the square root of the years traded.

byKey.days: You used days, not years. The Sharpe is annualised, so $T$ is in years.
byKey.full: You counted all 1,500 days. The first 249 cannot trade.

explain.text: The standard error is $1/\sqrt{4.96} = 0.45$, so 1.124 is 2.50 standard errors above zero. The 95% band runs from about 0.24 to 2.00. And that is for one pre-set rule; lesson 9's tuning would need a further haircut.

screens.title: An honest backtest
screens.prose: **No look-ahead.** Let $u_t$ be the position set at day $t$'s close, with hedge ratio $h_t$ fixed at entry. $$\text{P\&L}_t = u_{t-1}\big(\Delta y_t - h_{t-1}\,\Delta x_t\big) - c\,(\text{pounds traded at } t).$$ Here every $\alpha_t$, $\beta_t$ and sd comes from days up to $t$.
screens.question: A signal fires at day 400's close. When does the trade first earn or lose money?

options.text: On day 401, from day 400's close to day 401's close
On day 400
options.why: The trade happens at day 400's close, so day 400's move is already over. Earning it would be look-ahead.

options.text: From day 401's open
options.why: This backtest trades at closes. Moving to the next open is a different, also honest, convention.

feedback.correct: Correct. The trade earns from the next day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When is the position actually held?

explain.text: The position $u_{400}$ is set at day 400's close, so the first P&L it earns is $\Delta y_{401} - h\,\Delta x_{401}$. Day 400's own move happened before the trade. The Backtesting course's lesson 5 moves fills to the next open.

screens.question: Why does the desk care so much about costs for pairs in particular?

options.text: A pair crosses the spread on two legs at each open and close: about twice a one-share trade's cost
Pairs trade so rarely that costs never matter
options.why: B pays £2.64 of a £31.21 edge at 5 bp, and £10.58 at 20 bp.

options.text: Short sales are free, so only the long leg pays
options.why: Both legs cross a spread, and the short leg also pays a stock loan fee (the Markets course's lesson 12).

hints.text: How many shares does each pair trade touch?
Two legs, each crossing its own spread, at the open and at the close.
Two legs mean about twice the pounds traded per trade.

feedback.correct: Correct. Two legs double the bill, and shorting adds a loan fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the legs a pair trade crosses.

explain.text: Each change trades both $y$ and $\beta x$: about twice the pounds of a single share. At 20 bp the reference pair keeps £20.63 of £31.21. The Backtesting course's lesson 8 builds the change-the-future test for any strategy.

ideas: No look-ahead: every number used on day $t$ comes from days up to $t$. The trade happens at day $t$'s close and earns from day $t + 1$.
Fix the hedge ratio when a trade opens, and charge costs on both legs at every change. 5 bp takes £2.64 of the reference pair's £31.21.
Test a backtest by changing the future: the past P&L must not move. A full-sample fit fails, and inflates the Sharpe from 1.124 to 1.647.
